name: oblique_plane_through_three_points
why: The criterion of the entry to the letter: «the plane through three known points produces a plane whose normal is computed by hand and compared». Here the hand calculation is written in the case, and the operation redoes it on its own and compares it with what the plane says it is: the case checks the calculation, and the calculation checks the plane.
_why_a_skewed_plane_and_not_a_straight_o: On a plane parallel to a standard one the normal read by ROWS and the one read by COLUMNS come out equal, and a check made only that way would not tell the right reading from the wrong one -- it is the rule by which a case in which two wrong values give the same result tabulates nothing. The third point at (0, 100, 100) serves this: there the column would give (0, 0.7071, 0.7071), that is the normal turned.

expect.tolerance_why: the normalised cross product carries a square root of two: the sixth digit is rounding

expect.why: THE LINE THAT PROVES THE PLANE IS THE RIGHT ONE. If the third COLUMN were read instead of the third row, here (0, 0.7071, 0.7071) would come out: same magnitude, same form, direction turned by 90 degrees. On a straight plane the two readings coincide and nobody would notice.

expect.tolerance_why: it is the angle between the hand calculation and what SOLIDWORKS says: below a hundredth of a degree they are the same plane

expect.why: the plane really is in the tree, read from the state instead of from the answer of the operation
a reference plane is not material: if the volume changed, something else had been born

expect.tolerance_why: a horizontal plane: the numbers are exact, the tolerance is for the floating-point comparison
expect.why: the easy case, after the hard one: it serves to say that reading by rows is not a correction that breaks the straight planes to make the oblique ones come out right
